**Colombia's Constitutional Court — the judge who showed his working (2023–2024)**

In January 2023 a labour court judge in Cartagena ruled that a child with autism should not have to pay fees or transport costs for his therapies. What made the ruling famous was not the outcome but an appendix: the judge printed the questions he had put to ChatGPT, and its answers, inside the judgment itself. Colombian lawyers argued about it for months.

In August 2024 the Constitutional Court settled the argument in decision T-323. It did not overturn the ruling. The Court found the tool had not replaced the judge's function, because he had reached and reasoned his decision first and consulted the assistant afterwards, to broaden the argument. But it held that transparency and accountability had not been fully met, set out principles for any judge using these tools — among them non-substitution of human reasoning, verification, and human control — and directed the judiciary's governing council to issue guidance and training.

The distinction the Court drew is the one this lesson turns on. Think it through yourself, then bring the assistant in to widen the options, argue the other side and show you what you missed — and verify anything it hands back before you lean on it. Your decisions are smaller than a child's medical care, but the order matters no less: the reasoning stays yours, whoever helped you find it.

**The Supreme Court of India — 36,000 judgments, translated one checked step at a time (2023–2024)**

India's Supreme Court works in English, but most Indians do not read judgments in English. So the court set itself an enormous task: make its rulings readable in the languages people actually speak — eventually eighteen of them. Handing that over in one motion would have been reckless. A mistranslated line in a judgment is not a typo; it is somebody's rights described wrongly.

The Registry built it as a chain instead. A translation engine trained on judicial language produces the draft. That draft is then checked by people who know the material — court translators and retired judicial officers appointed for the purpose, with committees of sitting judges overseeing the work — and only the checked version is published on the court's public portal. Corrections made at the checking stage are fed back, so the next draft starts from a better place. The court has reported more than 36,000 judgments translated into Hindi and thousands more into sixteen other Indian languages, with languages added in stages rather than all at once.

Your chain is shorter and the stakes are lower, but the shape is identical: produce one piece, have it checked, feed what you learn back in, and only then move on. Notes, outline, draft, critique, polish. The step you will be tempted to skip is always the check — and it is always the cheapest place to fix anything.

**Aftonbladet — the newsroom that put its best prompts on a shelf (2023–2024)**

Sweden's largest daily set up an in-house AI team of eight people in October 2023, and ran into an ordinary problem straight away: a reporter would work out a genuinely good way to ask for something, use it once, and lose it by the following week. So the team began saving the good ones as small named tools — a collection the newsroom calls its AI Buffet. Spånaren takes an article link and suggests follow-up angles and questions. Buddy Reader reads a draft back and flags repetition, clumsy structure and weak reasoning. Another checks how well an article preview is written for search.

Each one is a prompt somebody refined once, given a name so the rest of the newsroom can take it off the shelf instead of rewriting it. The paper also taught the underlying skill: a course on prompting attended by more than 260 journalists. Deputy managing editor Martin Schori has been plain that shipping a tool is not the end of the job, pointing to the need for "consistent maintenance, data updates, and adjustments".

You are not building a newsroom toolbox. You are building five to ten templates in one document you will actually open on a Tuesday. The moves are identical: name the prompt that worked, put it somewhere a colleague can reach it, and edit it every time an output disappoints you.

**Autoriteit Persoonsgegevens — two pastes that became reportable data breaches (2024)**

In August 2024 the Dutch data protection authority issued a public warning, because organisations had begun reporting a new kind of breach: staff pasting other people's personal data into AI chatbots. In one case an assistant at a GP practice entered patients' medical details into a chatbot app. In another, an employee at a telecoms company pasted in a file of customer addresses. Neither was sabotage. Both were people trying to get through the day faster — and in both cases it went against agreements their employer had already made.

The consequence is the part worth carrying. The data left the organisation altogether: it sat on the technology company's servers, where it could be used to improve the software and where the practice could no longer reach it. "Once that information is in the system, you no longer have control of it," a spokeswoman for the regulator told Dutch media. Medical records carry extra protection in law, so sharing them without a lawful reason is a serious violation. The authority's instruction to employers was blunt: make clear agreements with staff about which tools may be used and what may be put into them.

Notice what that assistant actually needed — help summarising or phrasing, not the patients' names. This is the lesson in miniature: know the rule before you paste, strip the identifying details when you are unsure, and treat every paste as permanent, because it is.

**Yokosuka City — the city hall that started with the dullest paperwork in the building (2023)**

In April 2023 Yokosuka, a city in Kanagawa Prefecture, gave about 4,000 municipal staff — effectively everyone — access to ChatGPT for one month. Nothing visionary was attempted. Staff used it for drafting welfare-bulletin copy, summarising documents, proofreading and condensing meeting minutes: the paperwork nobody boasts about. The city even drafted the announcement of the trial with ChatGPT, then had staff proofread it before it went out.

Then Yokosuka did the part most organisations skip. It asked its own people, and reported the answer even though the answer was not flattering: around half of the staff surveyed said they were dissatisfied with the accuracy of what came back. It also measured the gain — the evaluation found the tool cut working time by at least ten minutes per employee per day. Weighing both, the city adopted it across the council in June 2023, kept the human proofreading step, and said it would seek expert advice on writing more effective prompts.

Read that sequence again, because it is your capstone in municipal form: a real recurring task, an honest look at what came back, a fix aimed at how they were asking rather than at the tool, and a way of working that survived to the following month. Those staff were not specialists. They were people with too much paperwork and one month to find out.

So pick your dullest recurring task, run it end to end, check it honestly, and keep the prompt that worked. That habit is what your certificate is for — and it will still be earning you time long after this course stops being new.
